chapter.title: Every hose on the street: Europe, 1944 to 1945

cards.body:
Within 16 days in June 1944, Germany was hit from both sides: the Allies landed in France on the 6th, and the Soviet army smashed through in the east on the 22nd. On our street, the fire has been driven back into the house where it started. Now there are hoses at the front door, the back door and the roof.

**A fire with nowhere left to run goes out.**
cards.simpler: Within 16 days in June 1944, Germany was attacked from two sides. On the 6th, the Allies landed in France. On the 22nd, the Soviet army broke through in the east. Think of our street. The fire has been pushed back into the house where it started. Now there are hoses at the front door, the back door and on the roof. **A fire with nowhere left to run goes out.**

cards.prompt: You're the fire chief. Your crew sprays the front door, and the fire just pulls back into the back rooms, then creeps out again. What ends it fastest?

options.text: A bigger hose at the front door.
Hoses at the front and the back at the same time.
Step back and let it burn itself out.

whyNot.a: That's one stronger hose, not two: the fire just keeps retreating to the rooms you can't reach.
whyNot.c: That's the 1938 hope, not the 1944 plan: this fire had burned for five years and showed no sign of stopping on its own.

cards.reteach: A fire, like an army, survives by moving its strength to wherever it isn't being hit. Hit it from two sides and every room it runs to is already under water. That's what 1944 did to Germany.

cards.title: Front door, back door, water main
cards.body:
On 6 June 1944, about 156,000 Allied soldiers landed on five beaches in Normandy, in northern France. That was the front door. **Germany now had to fight on two sides at once**, with the Soviet army already pushing in at the back.

You'd think D-Day was the bigger blow. In numbers, the east was: most German soldiers who died in the war died fighting the Soviets.

Behind both fronts ran the water main: factories. One American shipyard built a cargo ship in under five days, as a record attempt. Bombers, meanwhile, hit German fuel plants and cities from above.
cards.simpler: On 6 June 1944, about 156,000 Allied soldiers landed on five Normandy beaches in northern France. That was the front door. With the Soviets at the back door, **Germany now had to fight on two sides at once**. In numbers, the east hurt more: most German soldiers killed in the war died fighting the Soviets. Factories were the water main. One American shipyard built a cargo ship in under five days, as a record try. Bombers hit Germany's fuel plants and cities.

cards.title: The army made of rubber
cards.body: The Germans were sure the landing would come at Calais, where the Channel is narrowest. The Allies helped them believe it. In south-east England they parked a fake army, with *inflatable tanks*, dummy landing craft and busy radio chatter, and let the Germans think George Patton was leading it. Even after Normandy, Hitler kept a whole army waiting near Calais for weeks, guarding against the **real invasion that was already ashore**.
cards.simpler: The Germans were sure the landing would come at Calais, where the sea between England and France is narrowest. The Allies helped them believe it. In south-east England they set up a fake army, with blow-up rubber tanks, dummy landing boats and busy radio chatter. They let the Germans think George Patton was in charge of it. Even after Normandy, Hitler kept a whole army waiting near Calais for weeks, guarding against the **real invasion that was already ashore**.

cards.prompt: Autumn 1944. A German general finds 10 spare divisions (big army units of thousands of men each). Where can he send them without making things worse?

options.text: West, to push the Americans and British back into the sea.
East, to hold back the Soviets, the bigger threat.
Nowhere safe: every unit sent to one front leaves the other one thinner.

whyNot.a: That's fighting one hose, not two: weaken the east and the bigger Soviet army pours in through the back door.
whyNot.b: That's half the picture, not the squeeze: weaken the west and the Allies in France race for the river Rhine.

cards.reteach: Two fronts means every choice is a loss. Germany didn't have enough men to be strong in both places at once. The Allies made sure of that by attacking from both sides in the same summer.

cards.title: Why it took until May
cards.body:
So why did Germany hold out until May 1945? Mostly because one man would not quit.

**The surrender came only after the two fronts met and Hitler was dead.** American and Soviet soldiers shook hands on the river Elbe on 25 April. Hitler killed himself in Berlin on 30 April. Germany signed the surrender on 7 May, and it took effect on 8 May.

As they advanced, the armies found what Germany had been doing behind its fronts: Auschwitz in January, Bergen-Belsen in April, about six million Jews murdered.
cards.simpler: Germany held out until May 1945 mostly because Hitler would not quit. **The surrender came only after the two fronts met and Hitler was dead.** Americans and Soviets shook hands on the river Elbe on 25 April. Hitler killed himself on 30 April. Germany signed the surrender on 7 May, and it took effect on 8 May. As they advanced, the armies found the camps, like Auschwitz and Bergen-Belsen. About six million Jews had been murdered.

cards.body: Tom watches a D-Day film and tells a friend the Americans and British beat Germany in 11 months. The friend asks one question: where did most German soldiers die? In the east, fighting the Soviets. **If your story of 1944 has only one front, you've left out a hose.**
cards.simpler: Tom watches a film about D-Day. Then Tom tells a friend that the Americans and British beat Germany in 11 months. The friend asks just one question: where did most German soldiers die? The answer is in the east, fighting the Soviets. It's like praising the hose at the front door and forgetting the one at the back. **If your story of 1944 has only one front, you've left out a hose.**

cards.prompt: Germany was clearly losing by August 1944. Why did the surrender only come on 8 May 1945?

options.text: Hitler refused to quit, so it took both fronts closing in until they met, and his death eight days earlier.
D-Day took 11 months to finish landing all the troops.
Germany's factories finally ran out of materials that exact week.

whyNot.b: That's mixing up the landing and the squeeze: D-Day was one day, and the 11 months were the two fronts closing in.
whyNot.c: That's the factory story, not the ending: factories wore Germany down, but the surrender came after the fronts met and Hitler was gone.

cards.reteach: Losing and surrendering are not the same thing. Germany lost ground for 11 months, but Hitler would not stop while he lived. The surrender came only after the hoses met in the middle, at the river Elbe, and he was dead.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
After June 1944, Germany was squeezed from the west by D-Day, from the east by a bigger Soviet army and from above by bombers, all fed by Allied factories it could never match. **It held out mostly because Hitler refused to quit, and it surrendered about a week after his death.**

Tomorrow: the last house still burning, and why Japan's surrender is still argued about.
cards.simpler: After June 1944, Germany was squeezed from three sides. D-Day pushed in from the west. A bigger Soviet army pushed in from the east. Bombers hit from above. All of them were supplied by Allied factories that Germany could never keep up with. **It held out mostly because Hitler refused to quit, and it surrendered about a week after his death.** Tomorrow: the last house still burning, and why people still argue about Japan's surrender.

cards.body: Open the map app on your phone. Measure Cologne to Berlin, then Kostrzyn, on the Polish border, to Berlin. In March 1945 those were roughly where the two fronts stood. You'll see who was knocking first.
cards.simpler: Open the map app on your phone. Measure the distance from Cologne to Berlin. Then measure from Kostrzyn, a town on the Polish border, to Berlin. In March 1945, those two places were roughly where the two fronts stood. Compare the two lines, the way you might check which of two neighbours lives closer to your door. **You'll see who was knocking first.**

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now describe how Germany was squeezed from two sides in its last 11 months of war, and why it surrendered in May 1945, not earlier or later.

dubious_claims: 'That was what the war had been against': the Allies did not go to war to stop the Holocaust, and saying so rewrites what they were fighting for.

Exercise 3, option a, says 'both fronts closing on Berlin', and the reteach says the hoses met 'at the Elbe and in Berlin'. Only the Soviets took Berlin; the Americans and British stopped at the Elbe.
'The war in Europe ended only when the two fronts met and Hitler was dead' makes a simple cause-and-effect claim the chapter doesn't back up. Fine as a teaching shortcut, but it's stated as fact.
'Germany surrendered on 8 May' is fine as VE Day, but the first surrender was signed at Reims on 7 May and took effect on 8 May.
repairedFrom.why: Card 6 fits a second idea (Hitler refusing to quit) plus the bomb plot, the Elbe, his suicide, the surrender and the Holocaust into about 108 words, so the camps get two rushed lines with a misleading moral framing.
repairedFrom.fix: Cut the briefcase-bomb story and end on the two fronts meeting at the Elbe. Then give the camps their own sentence without 'That was what the war had been against', for example: 'As they advanced, the armies found what Germany had been doing behind its fronts: Auschwitz in January, Bergen-Belsen in April, about six million Jews murdered.'
